text: A psalm of David, when he fled from his son Absalom.
LORD, how many are my foes! How many rise up against me!
Many are saying of me, "There is no help for him in God." Selah

versions.text: Many are saying of me, "God will not deliver him." Selah
versions.explanation: The Hebrew is a denial that salvation exists for him *in God* (אֵין יְשׁוּעָתָה לּוֹ בֵאלֹהִים). The current rendering turns the taunt into a simple prediction and loses the emphatic 'in God,' which is the point of the mockery.

text: But you, LORD, are a shield around me, my glory, the one who lifts my head high.
I call aloud to the LORD, and he answers me from his holy mountain. Selah
I lie down and sleep; I wake again, because the LORD sustains me.
I will not fear the tens of thousands of people ranged against me on every side.

versions.text: I will not fear the tens of thousands drawn up against me on every side.
versions.explanation: The noun עָם ('people') is not represented in the translation; 'tens of thousands' alone leaves the object vague. Adding 'of people' restores the sense without harming the rhythm.

text: Rise up, LORD! Save me, my God! For you have struck all my enemies on the jaw; you have broken the teeth of the wicked.

versions.text: Rise up, LORD! Save me, my God! You strike all my enemies on the jaw; you shatter the teeth of the wicked.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew verbs are perfects introduced by כִּי ('for'), giving the ground of the appeal: past acts of deliverance. The present-tense rendering also drops the causal connector, weakening the logic of the prayer.

text: Deliverance belongs to the LORD. May your blessing rest on your people. Selah
